response.content:
# Write-Ahead Logging

## The WAL Invariant and Buffer Management Policies

The foundational rule of write-ahead logging is deceptively simple: no data page may be written to stable storage until the log records describing the changes to that page have themselves been durably written. This is the WAL invariant, sometimes decomposed into two sub-rules. First, "force log at commit" (also called the commit rule): before a transaction's commit can be acknowledged to the client, the commit log record and everything preceding it in that transaction's log chain must be flushed to durable storage. Second, the more general log-flush-before-page-flush rule applies to every update, not just commits: the LSN of the log record describing a page modification must be flushed before the corresponding modified page is allowed to reach disk.

This invariant exists because the log is the single source of truth for recovery. If a dirty page reaches disk before its log record, and the system crashes, there's no way to know the page was ever modified in a recoverable way — you'd have an unlogged state change baked into stable storage with no provenance. Conversely, if the log record is durable but the page update is lost, recovery can always replay (redo) the change, because the log record is self-describing.

This leads to the classic buffer management policy taxonomy, independent axes that every WAL-based engine must choose on:

- **Steal / no-steal**: "Steal" means the buffer manager is allowed to write an uncommitted (dirty) page to disk, typically under buffer pressure, before the transaction that modified it commits. Steal is almost universally adopted in real systems because disallowing it (no-steal) would require keeping every dirty page of every active transaction pinned in the buffer pool, which is infeasible for long transactions. Steal necessitates an undo mechanism during recovery, since a crash may leave disk pages reflecting uncommitted work.
- **Force / no-force**: "Force" means all pages modified by a transaction are flushed to disk synchronously at commit time. No-force defers those writes, relying on the log (and the redo pass) to reconstruct them if a crash occurs before the buffer manager naturally writes them back. Virtually all high-performance systems use no-force, since forcing pages at commit would mean random synchronous I/O proportional to the transaction's working set, whereas log flushes are sequential and cheap. No-force necessitates a redo mechanism.

ARIES, and essentially every production engine (InnoDB, PostgreSQL, SQL Server), is built on the steal/no-force combination, because it decouples transaction commit latency (bounded by a sequential log flush) from buffer pool eviction policy (which can write pages back whenever convenient, batched and reordered for efficiency).

## Log Sequence Numbers and Page-Log Ordering

Every log record is assigned a monotonically increasing LSN, typically the byte offset of the record within the logical (possibly multi-file) log stream, which conveniently makes LSNs totally ordered and usable directly as a seek position. Two LSN-based bookkeeping fields tie the log to the data pages:

- **PageLSN**: every data page stores, in its header, the LSN of the most recent log record that modified it. This is the crux of the physical-consistency check during redo: when recovery considers whether to reapply a log record to a page, it compares the log record's LSN to the page's PageLSN. If PageLSN ≥ the record's LSN, the update is already reflected on the page (it reached disk before the crash) and redo is skipped — this is what makes ARIES redo idempotent and safe to reapply even over an already-current page image.
- **RecLSN / RecoveryLSN** and the **flushed LSN (durable LSN)** watermark: the log manager tracks the LSN up to which the log buffer has been durably flushed. The WAL invariant is enforced mechanically by comparing a page's PageLSN against this flushed-LSN watermark before permitting the page to be written out — if PageLSN exceeds the flushed LSN, the log must be flushed first.

This PageLSN/flushed-LSN pair is what allows WAL to support no-force, steal buffer management without ever violating the invariant: it's checked at the moment of eviction, not enforced by forcing earlier writes.

## ARIES: Analysis, Redo, Undo

ARIES (Algorithm for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics) is the de facto standard recovery algorithm, and its three-pass structure is worth understanding precisely because each phase has a distinct purpose and distinct termination condition.

**Analysis pass.** Starting from the most recent checkpoint, analysis scans forward through the log to reconstruct two pieces of volatile state that were lost on crash: the Transaction Table (list of transactions that were active at crash time, each with its last-written LSN) and the Dirty Page Table, DPT (pages that may have uncommitted/unflushed changes, each annotated with a RecLSN — the LSN of the earliest log record that could have made that page dirty since its last flush). By the end of analysis, the system knows which transactions need undoing (those without a commit or abort record) and the lowest LSN from which redo must start (the minimum RecLSN across the DPT), called the redo point.

**Redo pass.** Starting at the redo point (not the beginning of the log — this is the main efficiency win from checkpointing), ARIES replays every logged update, including those belonging to transactions that will later be undone. This is counterintuitive but important: ARIES redoes everything unconditionally (subject to the PageLSN check described above) to first bring the database to exactly the physical state it was in at the moment of the crash, including the effects of losing transactions. Only afterward does undo roll back the losers. This "redo history, then undo losers" structure is what allows ARIES to use physiological logging and page-oriented redo without needing to reconstruct a logical, transaction-consistent intermediate state.

**Undo pass.** Walking backward through the log (following each loser transaction's PrevLSN chain, not a second forward scan), ARIES compensates for every update made by a transaction that never committed. Each undo action is itself logged, as a Compensation Log Record (CLR). Critically, CLRs point forward via an UndoNextLSN field to the next record to undo, skipping over the record just undone — this is what guarantees undo recovery terminates even if the system crashes repeatedly during undo itself: on a repeated crash, analysis re-finds the loser transaction, and undo resumes from the UndoNextLSN rather than redoing already-undone work, giving ARIES its idempotent, crash-safe-during-recovery property. CLRs are never themselves undone, which is what bounds the amount of undo work — you never undo an undo.

## Physiological vs. Physical vs. Logical Logging

Pure physical logging records exact before/after byte images of a page region. It's simple and makes redo trivial (just overwrite the bytes) but is wasteful and, worse, doesn't compose well with operations whose physical effect depends on the page's exact layout (e.g., inserting into a slotted page shifts other slots).

Pure logical logging records the logical operation ("insert key K with value V into index I"). It's compact and natural for undo (the inverse operation is also logical: "delete key K"), but it's dangerous for redo in the presence of partial page updates and concurrent structure changes, because reapplying a logical operation idempotently requires knowing precisely whether it was already applied, which in turn requires page-level information logical records don't carry.

ARIES's answer, and what's used in practice, is **physiological logging**: a log record identifies a specific page (physical addressing — so redo/undo target the right place) but describes the change at a logical level within that page (e.g., "insert this record into slot position determined by the page's current layout," rather than "write these exact bytes at this exact offset"). This gets the best of both: redo/undo can be applied against whatever the current physical layout of the page happens to be, which matters enormously for variable-length records and slotted pages, while still being anchored to a specific page via PageLSN checks for idempotence.

Log record types in a real ARIES-style log typically include: update records (physiological before/after or redo/undo images), commit records, abort records, CLRs (the undo-logging construct described above), and checkpoint-related records. CLRs deserve emphasis as a mechanism: they're never undone themselves, they carry an UndoNextLSN, and their existence is what bounds the log's growth during undo and makes crash-during-recovery safe.

## Checkpointing

Without checkpoints, recovery would need to scan the entire log from the beginning after every crash, which is unbounded in cost as a system runs longer. A checkpoint establishes a bounded starting point for analysis.

**Fuzzy checkpointing** is the standard mechanism (as opposed to a consistent/sharp checkpoint, which would require quiescing all activity and flushing all dirty pages — unacceptable for availability). A fuzzy checkpoint writes a checkpoint record containing a snapshot of the current Transaction Table and Dirty Page Table, but does not force those dirty pages to disk at checkpoint time. It only records their identities and RecLSNs. Because it doesn't need to block on I/O, a fuzzy checkpoint is cheap and fast, and can be taken frequently (e.g., time-based, every N minutes, or log-volume-based).

The DPT recorded at checkpoint time is exactly what analysis uses to compute the redo point (the minimum RecLSN), which is why checkpoint frequency directly bounds recovery time: redo never needs to scan further back than the oldest RecLSN of any page dirty at the last checkpoint. A master record (stored in a fixed, well-known location, separate from the log stream itself) points to the LSN of the most recent completed checkpoint so that restart can find it without scanning.

## Group Commit and Log Buffer Flushing

Because every commit requires a durable log flush, and flushes typically involve fsync-class calls with meaningful fixed latency, naively flushing per-transaction serializes commit latency across all concurrent transactions. **Group commit** batches the flush: multiple transactions' commit records (and preceding log records) accumulate in the log buffer, and a single flush operation durably persists all of them at once, after which all the batched transactions are acknowledged as committed together. This trades a small amount of added latency per individual transaction (waiting briefly to batch) for dramatically higher throughput under concurrency, since the fixed cost of an fsync is amortized across many transactions. Most production systems implement this via a configurable flush interval or triggered by buffer occupancy, and it composes directly with the force-at-commit rule: group commit doesn't violate the rule, it just batches *when* qualifying flushes happen and who gets to ride along on one physical I/O.

Log buffers themselves are typically implemented as circular in-memory buffers with multiple outstanding flush requests coalesced; the log manager must track the durable LSN watermark carefully so that the PageLSN check used by buffer eviction (described above) remains correct under this batching.

---

# LSM Trees

## Memtables and the Flush Path

An LSM tree accepts all writes into an in-memory, sorted structure called the memtable (commonly a skip list, as in LevelDB/RocksDB, or a balanced tree), which supports efficient ordered insertion and in-order iteration. Reads merge the memtable with on-disk state, and because the memtable is sorted, point lookups and range scans against it are efficient.

When the memtable reaches a size threshold, it's frozen as an **immutable memtable** and a new, empty, mutable memtable is swapped in to accept subsequent writes — this swap is the mechanism that lets writes continue uninterrupted while the frozen memtable is asynchronously flushed. The immutable memtable is then flushed to disk as a new SSTable (Sorted String Table) via a single sequential write, since the memtable is already sorted — flushing is a simple linear walk, not a sort. This immutable-memtable staging is important because it decouples the latency of accepting new writes from the latency of the (comparatively slow, I/O-bound) flush operation; without it, a flush-in-progress would have to block new writes or require much more complex concurrent-mutation logic on the structure being flushed.

## SSTable Structure, Block Indexes, and Merge Iterators

An SSTable is an immutable, sorted, on-disk file of key-value pairs, typically organized into fixed-size data blocks (e.g., 4-64 KB), each holding a run of sorted key-value pairs, often with key-prefix compression within the block since adjacent keys share prefixes. A sparse **block index** maps the first (or last) key of each block to that block's file offset, so a point lookup binary-searches the sparse index to find the candidate block, then scans or binary-searches within that one block — this avoids needing a dense in-memory index of every key, trading a bit of extra I/O (reading the whole candidate block) for a dramatically smaller index memory footprint. Many implementations add a per-block or per-file **bloom filter** (see below) and sometimes a secondary index layer (index blocks forming a small internal tree, as in RocksDB's two-level indexing) for very large files.

Because data for a given key range is spread across the memtable and multiple SSTables (across multiple levels or tiers), range scans and even point lookups require merging: a **merge iterator** (k-way merge, typically implemented with a heap/priority queue keyed by current key, with tie-breaking by recency, i.e., memtable beats newer SSTables beats older SSTables) presents the union of all these sorted sources as a single sorted logical stream, resolving duplicate keys by preferring the most recent write and discarding shadowed older versions and tombstoned keys on the fly. This merge iterator is the core read-path mechanism of every LSM implementation, and its efficiency (how many sources must be consulted) is exactly what compaction strategies are designed to bound.

## Compaction: Leveled vs. Tiered

Compaction exists to bound the number of SSTables (and thus sources a merge iterator or bloom-filter check must consult), to reclaim space from overwritten/deleted keys, and to maintain the sortedness invariant across levels.

**Leveled compaction** (the LevelDB/RocksDB default model) organizes SSTables into levels L0, L1, L2, ... with exponentially increasing size (commonly 10x per level). Within L1 and below, SSTables at a given level have non-overlapping key ranges, so a point lookup needs to check at most one SSTable per level (plus L0, which is special — see below). Compaction picks an SSTable at level L whose key range overlaps some set of SSTables at level L+1, merges them via the merge-iterator mechanism, and writes new, non-overlapping SSTables into L+1, discarding the inputs. This bounds **read amplification** well (lookup touches O(number of levels) SSTables, i.e., O(log of data size)) and bounds **space amplification** well (because compaction continuously rewrites and consolidates, obsolete/overwritten data is reclaimed promptly, typically keeping space overhead to roughly 10% over the logical data size). The cost is **write amplification**: each key may be rewritten many times as it's promoted through levels (classically cited as 10x or more cumulative rewrite factor), since a single compaction at level L rewrites all overlapping data at L+1 even if only a small fraction of keys actually changed.

**Tiered (size-tiered) compaction** (the Cassandra/HBase-style default, also an option in RocksDB) instead groups SSTables of similar size into tiers, and when enough SSTables of similar size accumulate at a tier, they're merged together into one larger SSTable at the next tier — but unlike leveled compaction, SSTables within the same tier can have fully overlapping key ranges, and compactions don't propagate exhaustively to the next tier every time. This substantially reduces **write amplification** (data is rewritten fewer times overall, since merges happen less eagerly and with larger batches), but at the cost of both **read amplification** (a point lookup may need to check many overlapping SSTables across tiers, since there's no non-overlap guarantee) and **space amplification** (obsolete versions linger longer before being merged away, and transient space spikes occur because a full tier's worth of old SSTables must coexist with the new merged one during compaction).

This read/write/space-amplification triangle is the central trade-off of LSM compaction design, and most real systems (RocksDB especially) expose it as a tunable choice per use case: write-heavy workloads lean tiered, read-heavy or space-constrained workloads lean leveled, and hybrid schemes exist (e.g., RocksDB's "leveled with tiered L0" hybrid, where L0 accumulates flushed memtables in a tiered fashion before being compacted down into a strictly leveled L1+).

## Bloom Filters

Because a point lookup for a non-existent key would otherwise require checking every SSTable that might contain it (bounded but still nontrivial under tiered compaction, and nonzero even under leveled compaction), each SSTable typically carries a **bloom filter**: a space-efficient probabilistic set-membership structure, a bit array with k hash functions, that can definitively say "key is absent" with zero false negatives, or "key is possibly present" with a tunable false-positive rate (typically tuned to ~1%, costing roughly 10 bits per key at that rate). On a lookup, the merge-iterator / read path consults each candidate SSTable's bloom filter before doing any actual disk I/O against it; a negative result lets that SSTable be skipped entirely. This is what makes point lookups in LSM trees practical despite data being fragmented across many files — without bloom filters, lookups for non-existent keys would be pathologically expensive relative to B-tree equivalents. The trade-off is the false-positive rate (wasted I/O on a small fraction of lookups) against memory consumed by the filter bits, and the fact that bloom filters must be rebuilt (not incrementally updatable in the simple case) whenever an SSTable is rewritten, which happens naturally during compaction anyway.

## Tombstones and Compaction-Time Garbage Collection

Because SSTables are immutable, a delete cannot simply remove a key from existing files — instead a **tombstone** record is written (to the memtable, then eventually flushed like any other record) marking the key as deleted, carrying the key and a sequence number/timestamp but no value. Reads via the merge iterator treat a tombstone as shadowing any older version of the same key from less-recent sources, and surface "not found" to the caller rather than the tombstone itself.

Tombstones must eventually be physically removed, which only happens during compaction, and only once the compaction process can prove no older version of that key could still be "exposed" by removing the tombstone — i.e., the tombstone has propagated down to (or past) the level/tier containing the oldest possible version of that key, or it has existed longer than any possible open snapshot/iterator that might still need to see it (a correctness subtlety tying tombstone GC to the snapshot/MVCC mechanism of the engine). Until that point, deleting a key can transiently *increase* space usage (the tombstone itself is a small write) and increase read-side cost (the merge iterator must still check sources below the tombstone to confirm nothing older is being incorrectly exposed, bounded in leveled schemes but potentially expensive in tiered schemes with deep, overlapping tiers). This tombstone-accumulation problem is one of the operationally trickiest aspects of LSM-based engines, particularly under tiered compaction or with long-lived, old SSTables that rarely get selected for compaction (the "orphaned tombstone" problem), and most production systems expose explicit tuning (e.g., Cassandra's `gc_grace_seconds`, RocksDB's periodic/forced compaction options) to bound how long this can persist.

## WAL's Role Specific to LSM Engines

Despite memtables living entirely in memory, LSM engines still need durability for writes that have been acknowledged but not yet flushed to an SSTable, since the memtable itself is volatile. The standard mechanism is the same WAL invariant as in page-based systems, applied in miniature: before (or atomically with) inserting a record into the memtable, the record is appended to a write-ahead log on durable storage, and the write is only acknowledged to the client once that log append is durably flushed (again, subject to force-at-commit-style semantics, and group-commit-style batching is common here too for throughput). This WAL is logically distinct from, and serves a different purpose than, the SSTables: it's purely a durability/crash-recovery mechanism, replayed (redone) into a fresh memtable on restart if the engine crashes before a flush occurred, and it's truncated/recycled once the corresponding memtable has been safely flushed into an SSTable (at that point the data's durability is guaranteed by the SSTable itself, and the log segment is redundant). Because this WAL is append-only and sequential by construction, it imposes much lower write latency than random-access durability would, which is part of why LSM engines achieve high write throughput generally — the "write-optimized" character of LSM trees comes from both the sequential WAL append and the batched, sequential nature of memtable flushing and compaction, as opposed to the random-access in-place writes characteristic of B-tree engines.

# B+Tree Maintenance

## Node Splits, Merges, Underflow/Overflow, and Fill Factor

A B+tree maintains the invariant that every node (except possibly the root) holds between some minimum and maximum number of keys, commonly expressed via an order or branching factor, and all leaves are at the same depth. An insertion that would push a node's key count past its maximum triggers a **split**: the node's keys are divided roughly in half, a new sibling node is allocated for the upper half, and the separator key (the first key of the new right node, or a copy of it in a leaf-anchored B+tree) is inserted into the parent, which may itself overflow and split recursively, potentially propagating all the way to the root — a root split is the only case that increases tree height. Deletion that would push a node below its minimum occupancy triggers **underflow handling**, resolved either by **merging** with a sibling (concatenating the two nodes' contents into one and removing the now-empty node and its separator key from the parent, which may itself underflow and merge recursively) or by **redistribution** (borrowing some keys from a sibling that has slack above the minimum, avoiding a merge and the parent-level update that would otherwise cascade).

Most production implementations deliberately avoid being maximally aggressive about immediate rebalancing: a common relaxation is to tolerate underflow down to some lower bound (e.g., allow a node to be up to 50% full, rather than merging the instant occupancy drops below 100%) and defer merges, because overly eager rebalancing on every single deletion causes excessive node churn and log volume (each merge/split is itself a structure modification that must be made durable) for workloads with delete/insert cycling on similar keys. The **fill factor** (target occupancy at insertion/bulk-load time, commonly ~70-90%, intentionally leaving slack rather than packing nodes to 100%) exists precisely to reduce the frequency of splits under subsequent insertion-heavy workloads: a node packed to 100% splits on the very next insert into it, whereas a node left at 70% fill has headroom to absorb further inserts before a split is needed. This is a direct space-for-write-amplification trade-off, conceptually analogous to the leveled-compaction trade-offs in LSM trees, though operating at a much finer grain.

## Latch Coupling (Crabbing)

Concurrent traversal and modification of a B+tree requires protecting against readers and writers observing an inconsistent tree mid-restructuring. The classical mechanism is **latch coupling**, also called crabbing: a traversal acquires a latch (a short-duration, in-memory mutual-exclusion primitive, distinct from a transactional lock, which typically protects logical rows/keys for the duration of a transaction rather than a single operation) on the current node before acquiring the latch on the child it's about to descend into, and only releases the parent's latch once the child's latch is safely held — hence "crabbing," moving like a crab's claws, always holding two adjacent rungs before releasing the lower one.

For read-only traversals, this can be relaxed to pure descending latching with immediate release of the parent as soon as the child is latched, since a reader never needs to retrace upward. For writes (inserts/deletes that might split or merge), naive crabbing would require holding exclusive latches up the entire potential path, since a leaf-level insert might cascade a split all the way to the root. The standard optimization is **optimistic latch coupling**: descend holding only shared (read) latches, assuming no structural change will be needed, and only escalate to exclusive latches (re-traversing if necessary) if the leaf operation turns out to require a split or merge. This optimization matters enormously for throughput because splits/merges are rare relative to total insert/delete volume, so pessimistically exclusive-latching the whole path on every write would serialize concurrent writers unnecessarily.

## B-link Trees

A further refinement, the **B-link tree**, adds a right-sibling pointer to every node (leaf and internal) and a "high key" (the upper bound of keys that belong under this node) to each node's metadata. This allows a node split to be performed as two separate, independently-latched steps rather than one atomic operation spanning parent and child: first the node is split and the new right sibling is linked in via the sibling pointer (a purely local, single-node-latch operation), and only afterward, potentially after releasing the latch entirely and letting other operations proceed, is the separator key posted up into the parent. In the window between these two steps, a concurrent traversal that arrives at the (already-split) original node looking for a key that's now in the new right sibling can detect this via the high-key check (the sought key exceeds the node's high key) and simply follow the sibling pointer rightward to find it, rather than needing to find it via the parent. This is what gives B-link trees their defining property: searches never need to wait for a pending split's parent-update step to complete, because the sibling-pointer chain always provides a valid path to the data even in that intermediate state — hence "lock-free-ish" concurrent splits, since the exclusive latching window needed per split is reduced to a single node rather than a parent-child pair held simultaneously.

## Copy-on-Write vs. In-Place Update B-Trees

**In-place update** B-trees (the InnoDB model) modify pages directly in the buffer pool and write the same physical page location back to disk on flush, which is efficient in space (no page is ever duplicated) and allows tight integration with a physiological WAL as described earlier — the system logs the specific physiological change to the page and relies on redo/undo against that fixed page identity. This is efficient but requires careful latch coupling as above, and recovery must physically replay/undo changes to specific page slots using the WAL/ARIES machinery.

**Copy-on-write** B-trees (the LMDB model, and used in Couchbase's underlying storage, as well as conceptually in systems like BTRFS) never modify a page in place. Instead, any update to a leaf allocates a new copy of that leaf with the change applied, which forces a new copy of its parent (to update the pointer to the new leaf), cascading all the way up to a new root — meaning every write, even a single-key update, produces a new version of every node on the path from root to leaf. This sounds expensive, but it has a crucial payoff: the old root (and the entire old tree it points to) remains perfectly valid and untouched, so a reader holding a reference to the old root sees a fully consistent, unchanging snapshot with zero latching required against writers — this is what gives LMDB its single-writer/many-reader, latch-free-read concurrency model, and it's also what makes crash recovery nearly trivial: since old pages are never overwritten until explicitly reclaimed, a crash mid-write simply leaves the old root valid and the new, partially-written pages orphaned and ignorable, removing the need for a conventional WAL/redo-undo recovery protocol at all (LMDB famously has no WAL). The trade-offs are increased write amplification (one key change touches O(tree height) pages, not O(1)) and the need for a garbage-collection/page-reclamation mechanism (LMDB's free list) to reclaim old page versions once no reader snapshot still references them, conceptually analogous to tombstone GC and MVCC-driven garbage collection in LSM and other systems.

## Bulk Loading and Rebalancing

Inserting a large, pre-sorted dataset key-by-key via the normal insertion path is inefficient, causing a split cascade proportional to the dataset size. **Bulk loading** instead builds the tree bottom-up: data is sorted (if not already), leaves are packed sequentially at the target fill factor directly from the sorted stream (no split logic needed, since each leaf is filled to its target occupancy exactly once), and internal levels are built directly above the completed leaf level by grouping the leaves' separator keys, repeating until a single root remains. This is dramatically faster than iterative insertion (effectively O(n) sequential writes versus O(n log n) random-access-like split cascades) and produces a tree with ideal fill factor and no fragmentation, which is why bulk load is the standard mechanism for initial data loads, index (re)builds, and large batch imports. Online **rebalancing** of an already-built, live tree (as opposed to bulk load of fresh data) is comparatively rare as an explicit operation in most engines; most real systems rely on the organic split/merge mechanism above to keep the tree balanced incrementally rather than performing wholesale periodic rebalances, though some systems do offer an explicit "rebuild index" operation that's effectively a bulk-load pass used to reclaim fragmentation accumulated from many split/merge cycles over time (directly analogous to LSM compaction's role in reclaiming fragmentation from an LSM tree, though triggered manually/administratively rather than automatically).

## Structure Modification Operations and WAL Interaction

A page split or merge is a **structure modification operation (SMO)**: unlike an ordinary record insert/update/delete, which touches exactly one page, an SMO touches multiple pages (the splitting node, the newly allocated sibling, and the parent receiving the new separator key) that must be made durable and recoverable as an atomic unit despite spanning multiple page writes and multiple log records.

This interacts with physiological/physical logging in a specific way: because an SMO isn't a single atomic physical write, ARIES-style systems typically log it as a short sequence of log records (e.g., "allocate new page," "move upper half of keys from node A to new page B," "insert separator key for B into parent P"), and crucially mark the SMO as logically atomic with respect to recovery even though it isn't atomic with respect to the buffer manager — if a crash occurs mid-split, redo must be able to either complete or safely roll forward through the partial SMO so the tree is left structurally consistent (not with a dangling sibling pointer, missing separator key, or orphaned page), rather than naively redoing/undoing each constituent record independently as if unrelated. Some systems achieve this via a dedicated "SMO log record" that captures enough logical information to redo the whole operation idempotently as a unit, while others structure the sub-steps so that each intermediate state is independently well-formed (this is exactly the design motivation behind B-link trees' two-step split: because the right-sibling-link step is independently consistent, and the parent-separator-key-posting step is independently consistent, a crash between them leaves the tree in a valid, if suboptimal, state — a reader can still find everything via the sibling-pointer fallback — rather than requiring the whole SMO to be treated as one indivisible recovery unit). This is a direct instance of logical logging being favored over pure physical logging for exactly the reason discussed in the WAL section: the operation's meaning (split node A into A and B, insert separator in P) is far more compact and far more robust to concurrent physical layout changes than trying to physically log the exact byte-level transformation of three separate pages as if they were one unit.

# Concurrency Control and Recovery: MVCC and Crash Recovery

## 1. Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC)

### 1.1 Snapshot Isolation and Read View Construction

MVCC's foundational idea is that writers never block readers and readers never block writers, because each transaction operates against a *consistent snapshot* of the database rather than against the single, mutable current state that lock-based concurrency control schemes expose. A snapshot is a logical cut of the database as of some point in (logical) time, and every transaction that reads under snapshot isolation (SI) perceives only the versions of rows that were committed before that cut point, plus its own uncommitted changes.

The mechanics of snapshot construction differ by system but converge on two common primitives: transaction identifiers (XIDs) and commit timestamps/sequence numbers.

**PostgreSQL's approach** assigns every transaction a monotonically increasing XID when it first writes (virtual XIDs are used for read-only transactions to avoid XID space exhaustion). When a transaction begins (or, under `READ COMMITTED`, at the start of each statement), it takes a snapshot consisting of:
- `xmin`: the smallest XID still active (i.e., not yet committed or aborted) at snapshot time — transactions below this are guaranteed visible if committed.
- `xmax`: one past the highest XID assigned so far — transactions at or above this didn't exist yet and are invisible.
- A list of XIDs of all transactions that are concurrently in-progress at snapshot time.

A tuple version is visible to the snapshot if its inserting transaction committed before the snapshot was taken (determined by checking commit status in `pg_xact`/CLOG and comparing XIDs against the snapshot's xmin/xmax/in-progress list) and its deleting transaction (if any) either hasn't committed or is itself invisible. This is a form of *XID-interval visibility checking* — no actual wall-clock time is consulted; ordering is purely transactional.

**Oracle's approach** is conceptually similar but anchors visibility on the System Change Number (SCN), a monotonically increasing logical timestamp assigned at commit. A query captures the current SCN at start and reads the version of each block/row that was current as of that SCN, reconstructing older versions from undo segments when the on-disk block has been overwritten by a newer transaction.

**MySQL/InnoDB** builds the read view from a list of active transaction IDs (trx_ids) at the moment the view is created, plus `low_limit_id` (next trx_id to be assigned) and `up_limit_id` (smallest active trx_id). Each clustered index record carries a hidden `DB_TRX_ID`, and visibility is determined by walking the record's undo-log-linked version chain until a version is found whose creating transaction is either the current transaction or committed and not in the view's active list.

The critical trade-off of snapshot isolation is that it provides repeatable reads without read locks, at the cost of (a) needing to retain multiple physical versions of each row, and (b) not guaranteeing full serializability — it permits write skew (discussed in 1.4).

### 1.2 Version Chains and Tuple Versioning

MVCC requires that multiple physical versions of a logical row coexist, linked so that readers can locate the version visible to their snapshot. Two dominant architectural approaches exist:

**Append-only / in-place-with-header versioning (PostgreSQL).** Every heap tuple carries `xmin` (the XID of the inserting/updating transaction) and `xmax` (the XID of the deleting/updating transaction, or 0/invalid if still live), plus `cmin`/`cmax` command-ID fields to distinguish operations within the same transaction. An `UPDATE` in PostgreSQL does not modify a tuple in place; it marks the old tuple's `xmax` with the updater's XID and inserts an entirely new tuple with `xmin` equal to that XID, chained via the `ctid` pointer (and, for HOT updates, kept on the same page to avoid index maintenance). This produces a backward-linked version chain per logical row. The trade-off is heap bloat: every update leaves behind a dead tuple that must eventually be reclaimed, and indexes must be able to reach any version (or be revalidated) — mitigated by Heap-Only Tuples (HOT) when indexed columns are unchanged.

**Undo-log-based versioning (Oracle, InnoDB).** Here the base data structure (data block or clustered index page) is updated in place, and the *previous* version's image is pushed to an undo segment (Oracle) or undo log (InnoDB), with the live record carrying a pointer/roll-pointer back to its prior version. Readers needing an older snapshot must walk this undo chain, applying undo records to reconstruct the version as of their required SCN/read-view. This keeps the primary data structure compact (no proliferating dead row versions in the main heap/index) but makes visibility resolution for old snapshots more expensive (potentially long undo chains under long-running transactions and heavy concurrent writes) and introduces a hard dependency on undo retention: if required undo has been overwritten/purged, long-running queries fail with a "snapshot too old"-class error.

Both schemes share the invariant that version identity is tied to transaction identifiers (or the derived commit timestamp/SCN), and both must handle multiple versions created within a single transaction by multiple statements (command-ID / statement-level snapshots).

### 1.3 Garbage Collection of Old Versions

Because MVCC retains multiple versions, every implementation needs a mechanism to reclaim versions no longer visible to any present or future transaction.

**PostgreSQL VACUUM.** VACUUM scans heap pages (and can be invoked manually, via `autovacuum` daemons, or forced via `VACUUM FREEZE`) and reclaims dead tuples — those whose `xmax` is below the oldest XID that any currently active transaction's snapshot could still need to see (the "OldestXmin" horizon, tracked across the active transaction list, held replication slots, and prepared transactions). It also removes corresponding index entries, marks space as reusable in the free-space map, and (critically for long-term correctness) performs *freezing*: once a tuple's `xmin` is older than all possible active snapshots, it's marked frozen (`FrozenTransactionId`/freeze bits) so XID wraparound comparisons no longer apply to it — necessary because XIDs are a 32-bit wrapping counter and ambiguity would otherwise arise after ~2 billion transactions. Failure to vacuum aggressively enough under long-running transactions or replication slots holding back the horizon leads to catastrophic table/index bloat and, in the extreme, transaction ID wraparound data loss.

**Oracle undo retention / purge.** Oracle doesn't garbage-collect row versions in the primary structures (they're updated in place); instead it ages out undo segments according to `UNDO_RETENTION` or automatic undo management tuning, reclaiming undo extents once no active or (if flashback/undo-retention-guaranteed queries require it) potentially-needed transaction still references them. SMON (System Monitor) performs undo segment cleanup; purge of now-unnecessary undo is driven by the same low-water-mark logic as PostgreSQL's OldestXmin — identify the oldest SCN any live or guaranteed-retained query might need, and free everything older.

**InnoDB purge threads.** InnoDB runs dedicated background purge threads that process the history list (the linked list of undo log records for committed transactions) and physically remove delete-marked records and obsolete undo log entries once no active read view's "up_limit_id" could still require them. This is explicitly asynchronous and decoupled from transaction commit — commit only marks a transaction as "to be purged"; the purge threads reclaim space lazily, which is why a long-running transaction (holding an old read view) in InnoDB causes unbounded growth of the history list, analogous to PostgreSQL's vacuum-blocking long transactions.

In all three systems, the garbage collection horizon is fundamentally computed the same way: it is the minimum snapshot/XID/SCN across all transactions (and sometimes replicas or held slots) that could still legitimately need to see an old version. This ties GC design tightly to how the active transaction list / global visibility state is tracked and broadcast.

### 1.4 Write Skew and Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)

Snapshot isolation prevents many classical anomalies (dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and — contrary to the strict ANSI reading — even phantom reads in most real implementations), but it does **not** guarantee serializability. The canonical failure mode is **write skew**: two transactions T1 and T2 each read overlapping data, and each writes to a *disjoint* subset of that data based on what they read, such that each individual write is consistent with what was read, but the concurrent combination violates an invariant that would hold under any serial execution. The textbook example is two on-call doctors each checking "is at least one of us on call" and each independently deciding to go off call, because each reads a snapshot in which the other still appears on call — after both commit, zero doctors are on call, violating the invariant, even though neither transaction's individual before/after state was internally inconsistent.

Write skew is a consequence of SI's "read is from the past, write is to the future" structure combined with first-committer/first-updater-wins conflict detection that only catches *write-write* conflicts on the same row, never *read-write* conflicts across different rows.

**Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)**, as implemented in PostgreSQL's `SERIALIZABLE` isolation level and derived from the Cahill/Fekete/Röhm algorithm, augments plain SI with detection of **rw-antidependencies** — the situation where transaction T1 reads a version of a row and transaction T2 later (or concurrently) writes a version that T1's read "overwrites" in logical serial order (T1 read the old version, so in any equivalent serial order T1 must precede T2, giving an edge T1 → T2 in the precedence graph). SSI tracks these antidependency edges at runtime: every row read is tracked against subsequent (or prior, if the writer committed first) writes to the same row by other transactions, materialized via SIREAD locks (predicate-style read markers that don't block anything, just record "this transaction read this predicate/row version"). SSI then detects **dangerous structures**: specifically, a cycle or a "pivot" transaction with both an incoming and an outgoing rw-antidependency edge in the same commit window (T_in → T_pivot → T_out), which is the necessary condition proven by Cahill et al. for a serialization anomaly to exist in an SI history. When such a structure is detected, one of the participating transactions is aborted (serialization failure, requiring client-side retry), rather than performing a full, expensive construction of the complete serialization graph.

The engineering trade-off of SSI is that it preserves SI's optimistic, non-blocking read characteristics (readers still never block writers) while adding bookkeeping overhead (SIREAD lock/predicate tracking, with granularity escalation from tuple to page to table to limit memory) and a non-zero false-positive abort rate (dangerous structures are a conservative over-approximation of actual anomalies, so some aborted transactions would not actually have produced an anomaly). It's a middle ground between lock-based S2PL serializability (always correct, but readers and writers block each other) and plain SI (never blocks, but not serializable).

### 1.5 Timestamp Ordering (T/O) Concurrency Control

Timestamp ordering is a logically distinct scheduling discipline, sometimes used as MVCC's theoretical ancestor and sometimes layered under/alongside MVCC implementations (e.g., it's the conceptual basis for how many MVCC systems order versions even though they use optimistic snapshot techniques operationally). In basic T/O, every transaction Ti is assigned a unique timestamp TS(Ti) at start, and every data item X carries a read-timestamp RTS(X) and write-timestamp WTS(X) reflecting the timestamps of the last transactions to read/write it. The scheduler enforces that all operations execute in an order consistent with transaction timestamps:
- A `read(X)` by Ti is rejected (and Ti aborted/restarted with a new timestamp) if TS(Ti) < WTS(X) — Ti would be reading a value that, serially, should have been overwritten before Ti "happened."
- A `write(X)` by Ti is rejected if TS(Ti) < RTS(X) or TS(Ti) < WTS(X), using Thomas's Write Rule to allow safely ignoring (rather than aborting on) obsolete writes when TS(Ti) < WTS(X) but the read set isn't violated.

Basic T/O guarantees conflict serializability by construction (the timestamp order *is* the serialization order) without requiring locking, but its practical cost is a high abort/restart rate under contention, since any out-of-order arrival forces a restart rather than queuing (as 2PL would) or buffering a version (as MVCC would). This is precisely why production MVCC systems don't use pure basic T/O: by retaining multiple versions and allowing a read of X to be satisfied by whichever version of X has the largest WTS(X) ≤ TS(Ti) (**multiversion timestamp ordering, MVTO**), reads essentially never abort, and only writes need timestamp-ordering checks. This MVTO formulation is, in fact, the formal concurrency-control model that most closely matches what PostgreSQL/Oracle/InnoDB implement operationally with XIDs/SCNs standing in for timestamps — the "timestamp" is just not wall-clock but a logical commit counter. T/O-style thinking also underlies systems using hybrid logical clocks or true wall-clock timestamps (e.g., CockroachDB's hybrid-logical-clock timestamps, Google Spanner's TrueTime-based commit timestamps) to achieve externally consistent snapshot ordering across distributed nodes, where "timestamp" literally becomes a synchronized physical/logical clock reading rather than a counter.

### 1.6 Isolation Levels and Anomalies

Per the ANSI SQL-92 isolation level definitions (refined by subsequent critiques, notably Berenson et al.'s "A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels," which is the correct technical reference since the original ANSI text is ambiguous about phenomena like phantoms under different concurrency control implementations):

- **READ UNCOMMITTED**: permits dirty reads (reading uncommitted/aborted data of other transactions), non-repeatable reads, and phantoms. Rarely implemented faithfully in MVCC systems — PostgreSQL maps this to READ COMMITTED behavior since MVCC makes true dirty reads unnatural to implement.
- **READ COMMITTED**: prevents dirty reads (each statement/read sees only committed data) but permits non-repeatable reads (re-reading the same row within a transaction can see a different, later-committed value) and phantoms (re-running a range predicate can return different rows). MVCC implementations achieve this by taking a fresh snapshot per statement rather than per transaction.
- **REPEATABLE READ**: prevents dirty reads and non-repeatable reads by holding one snapshot for the whole transaction (in MVCC terms) or by holding read locks for the duration (in 2PL terms). Classically permits phantoms in lock-based implementations (new rows satisfying a predicate can appear, since range predicates aren't locked, only existing rows) — but note that most MVCC systems' REPEATABLE READ (PostgreSQL, MySQL/InnoDB) de facto also prevents phantoms as a side effect of snapshotting, *except* they still permit write skew, which the ANSI standard's phenomena table doesn't explicitly characterize since it predates SI research.
- **SERIALIZABLE**: prevents dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms, and write skew/lost updates, guaranteeing the execution is equivalent to some serial order. Achieved via strict two-phase locking (S2PL) with predicate/range locking (preventing phantoms by locking the predicate, not just rows), via SSI (snapshot plus rw-antidependency cycle detection, as above), or via deterministic/OCC scheduling in some distributed systems.

**Lost updates** (T1 reads X, T2 reads X, T1 writes X, T2 writes X based on its stale read, overwriting T1's write) are prevented by REPEATABLE READ in true MVCC systems via the first-updater-wins or first-committer-wins rule: when T2 attempts to update a row that has been concurrently modified by a since-committed T1, the engine detects the version conflict (the row's current `xmax`/version no longer matches what T2's snapshot read) and forces T2 to either retry against the new version (PostgreSQL's default for most commands) or abort with a serialization error. This conflict check is itself an MVCC-native mechanism distinct from SSI — it only catches direct write-write conflicts on the same row, which is why write skew (disjoint writes) slips through at REPEATABLE READ/SI but lost update (same-row writes) does not.

---

## 2. Crash Recovery

### 2.1 Failure Classification

Standard recovery theory (following Gray & Reuter, and the ARIES literature) classifies failures into three categories, each demanding a different recovery mechanism:

- **Transaction (local) failure**: an individual transaction cannot complete, due to a logic error, constraint violation, deadlock victim selection, or explicit `ROLLBACK`. Recovery is purely **undo**: reverse the transaction's own updates using the log, restoring affected pages to their pre-transaction state, without affecting other transactions or requiring a restart. This is handled identically whether or not a crash occurs — it's "online" rollback.
- **System failure**: a crash (power loss, OS panic, process kill) that destroys the contents of volatile memory (buffer pool) but leaves non-volatile storage (disk) intact, though disk may hold a mixture of pages from in-flight, committed, and uncommitted transactions at the instant of the crash, because the buffer manager flushes dirty pages asynchronously and out of transaction-commit order. This is where the **ARIES** algorithm (analysis, redo, undo — detailed in 2.2) is the canonical recovery mechanism: it must restore the database to a state reflecting exactly the effects of all committed transactions as of the crash, and none of the uncommitted ones.
- **Media (disk) failure**: non-volatile storage itself is partially or wholly destroyed/corrupted (disk head crash, bad sectors, accidental file deletion). Log-based redo/undo cannot help if the base data pages are physically gone. Recovery requires a strictly separate mechanism: restoring the most recent full/incremental **backup** and then applying the Write-Ahead Log (WAL)/archive log records generated since that backup to roll forward to the point of failure (or to a desired recovery point) — this is **media recovery**, and it's the mechanism underlying both standard "restore and roll forward" DBA procedures and continuous log-shipping replication (2.6).

The classification matters because each tier has a fundamentally different recovery time objective and mechanism: transaction failure recovery is instantaneous and local; system-failure recovery via ARIES is bounded by checkpoint interval (2.4); media failure recovery is bounded by backup frequency and log archive volume, and can be arbitrarily long if backups are old or archives are large.

### 2.2 ARIES: Analysis, Redo, Undo

ARIES (Algorithm for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics), developed at IBM and underlying most WAL-based systems' recovery (PostgreSQL's and InnoDB's recovery are both conceptually ARIES-derived, though not byte-for-byte identical), structures crash recovery as three sequential passes over the log following a system failure, built on the premise that WAL already guarantees every data page modification is preceded by a corresponding durable log record (the WAL protocol/rule: no dirty page is flushed to disk until its associated log record(s) are durably written, typically enforced via a page's `pageLSN` versus the flushed-LSN high-water-mark).

**Analysis pass**: scans forward from the most recent checkpoint's begin record to the end of the log, reconstructing two critical structures as they existed at crash time: the **Transaction Table** (every transaction that was active, i.e., had started but not yet committed/aborted-and-fully-undone, along with its `lastLSN`) and the **Dirty Page Table** (every page that may have been modified in buffer pool memory but not yet flushed to disk, along with the `recLSN` — the LSN of the earliest log record that could have dirtied it). At the end of analysis, the transaction table identifies exactly which transactions require undo (those not marked committed) and the dirty page table identifies the low-water-mark LSN from which redo must begin.

**Redo pass**: scans forward from the minimum `recLSN` across the dirty page table (not necessarily from the very start of the log — this is the checkpoint's benefit), and **repeats history unconditionally** for every logged update: it reapplies the physical/logical change described by each log record to the corresponding page, regardless of whether the owning transaction ultimately committed or will be undone. This is the crucial ARIES design decision — redo doesn't try to be selective about which transactions "deserve" redoing, because that would require knowing final transaction outcomes before examining the full log, and because it keeps the redo pass simple and purely mechanical. Any transaction that should not have survived gets undone afterward in the undo pass. Redo for a given record is skipped only if the page's on-disk `pageLSN` is already ≥ the log record's LSN, which is the idempotency check (2.3).

**Undo pass**: scans backward from the end of the log (using the transaction table's `lastLSN` chains per loser transaction) and undoes every update belonging to a transaction that was not committed at crash time, writing **Compensation Log Records (CLRs)** for each undo action. CLRs are themselves logged (so that if the system crashes again *during* recovery, the undo work already performed is not repeated) and contain a `NextUndoLSN` pointer that lets the undo pass skip directly past already-undone sections of a transaction's log chain if recovery is itself interrupted and restarted — guaranteeing recovery recovery terminates in bounded additional work rather than looping.

ARIES's relationship to WAL is that WAL is the *enabling invariant* (log records durable before data) while ARIES is the *consuming algorithm* that exploits that invariant to reconstruct correct state; WAL alone doesn't specify a recovery procedure, and ARIES without WAL's ordering guarantee would be unsound (redo/undo could be applied against pages whose preceding log wasn't actually durable). ARIES departs from naive "redo-only-committed, undo-only-at-commit" proposals specifically because it tolerates and expects pages to be written to disk by the buffer manager in a wholly different order than the log, and in a wholly different set than "transactions that committed," which is what makes the fuzzy-checkpoint/no-force buffer management strategy viable.

### 2.3 Idempotency and Repeating History

Redo must be idempotent because recovery itself can crash and restart arbitrarily many times, and because the same log record range may need to be scanned and reapplied across multiple analysis/redo cycles if a crash occurs during recovery. ARIES guarantees idempotency via **page LSNs**: every data page stores the LSN of the last log record that modified it (`pageLSN`). Before reapplying a log record with LSN L to a page during redo, the algorithm checks whether `pageLSN ≥ L`; if so, the update is already reflected on the page (it reached disk before the crash) and redo is skipped. This single comparison is what allows "repeating history" — blindly replaying the log forward — to be safe and correct rather than destructive: physical redo re-executes the exact same byte-level change the original operation performed, so reapplying it to a page already containing that change is a no-op, and reapplying it to a page missing the change correctly brings it current. Idempotency is also what makes it safe for the redo pass to not distinguish winner/loser transactions — redoing a to-be-undone transaction's effect and then undoing it in the subsequent pass is logically equivalent to never having redone it, provided undo itself is correctly logged via CLRs.

### 2.4 Checkpointing and Bounded Recovery Time

Without checkpoints, the analysis pass would need to scan from the beginning of the log, and recovery time would grow unboundedly with system uptime. A **checkpoint** establishes a more recent, safe starting point. ARIES specifically uses **fuzzy checkpointing**: rather than quiescing all activity and flushing every dirty page (a *sharp*/*consistent* checkpoint, which stalls the system and is impractical at scale), a fuzzy checkpoint simply records, at a point in time, the current Transaction Table and Dirty Page Table snapshots and writes a `begin_checkpoint`/`end_checkpoint` log record pair — it does not wait for dirty pages to actually be flushed. The checkpoint's `end_checkpoint` record's LSN, together with the dirty page table it captured (specifically the minimum `recLSN` among all dirty pages at that time), gives analysis an authoritative point from which to resume scanning, and gives redo its true starting LSN — which may be considerably earlier than the checkpoint itself if a page has been dirty in the buffer pool for a long time without being flushed. This is why some systems additionally bound buffer pool dirty-page age (e.g., forcing periodic background flushing of old dirty pages) to keep the effective redo start point from drifting too far behind the checkpoint, trading higher steady-state I/O for lower worst-case recovery time. Checkpoint frequency is thus a direct dial on recovery time objective (RTO): more frequent checkpoints shrink the log range that must be scanned/redone but add continuous overhead; this is the same trade-off expressed in PostgreSQL's `checkpoint_timeout`/`max_wal_size` and InnoDB's checkpoint-age-driven flushing.

### 2.5 Shadow Paging

Shadow paging is a historically significant alternative to WAL-based recovery that avoids undo/redo logging entirely by using copy-on-write semantics at the page level. The database maintains a **page table** mapping logical page numbers to physical disk locations. To modify a page, a transaction writes a new physical copy of the page (leaving the original, "shadow," copy untouched) and updates a *private, in-progress* copy of the page table to point to the new copy; the original, committed page table remains valid and visible to all other transactions throughout. On commit, the new page table is made current via a single atomic pointer/disk-block swap (writing the new page table's root location to a fixed, well-known disk location); on abort, the private page table copy is simply discarded and the original shadow pages remain authoritative, with zero undo work required.

The trade-offs relative to WAL/ARIES are substantial and are why shadow paging has been largely abandoned in mainstream systems: (1) it causes severe data fragmentation, since logically adjacent pages drift apart physically with every update, defeating sequential I/O locality; (2) it provides no natural support for fine-grained concurrency, because the copy-on-write page table swap is naturally transaction-wide/coarse (concurrent transactions modifying different parts of the database still contend on page table versions, making it awkward to interleave at sub-transaction granularity the way WAL/MVCC does); (3) garbage collection of old shadow pages after commit is itself a non-trivial background process (symmetric to vacuum/purge in MVCC, but for an entirely different reason — reclaiming superseded physical pages rather than superseded logical versions); (4) it does not naturally extend to media recovery / point-in-time recovery, since there's no sequential, replayable log of operations to ship or archive — only full page-table snapshots. WAL-based ARIES recovery, by contrast, supports fine-grained, high-concurrency, continuously-streamed recovery semantics, which is the decisive reason it displaced shadow paging in virtually all production RDBMSs (shadow paging survives mostly in specialized/historical contexts, e.g., some early filesystem designs and System R's original design).

### 2.6 Log Shipping and Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)

Because WAL is a complete, ordered, replayable record of all physical page changes, it can be treated as a transport mechanism for both replication and media recovery beyond simple crash recovery.

**Media recovery / PITR**: starting from a full base backup (a physical copy of all data files taken at some known LSN/checkpoint), an operator (or automated tooling) can replay archived WAL segments generated after that backup to reconstruct database state as of any desired target — the moment of a crash, a specific timestamp, a specific transaction ID, or a named restore point. This is only correct because of the same idempotency/repeat-history property that underlies crash recovery: applying archived WAL forward from a backup is structurally identical to the ARIES redo pass, just starting from a backup image instead of a buffer-pool-crash-state image, and (for a clean PITR to an exact point) followed by an undo pass for any transactions that were in-flight at the target recovery point and must be excluded. This gives PITR its core utility: recovering not just from crashes but from logical errors (accidental `DROP TABLE`, bad bulk update) by rolling forward only to just before the damaging transaction.

**Log shipping / streaming replication**: the same WAL stream that supports PITR can be continuously shipped to one or more standby/replica nodes, which continuously apply it (running what is architecturally a never-ending redo pass) to maintain a near-real-time hot or warm standby. This conflates recovery and replication mechanisms deliberately — a replica is, at any instant, a database "recovering" from a backup via an unbounded log replay, and promoting a replica to primary after a primary failure is operationally a recovery event (the replica must finish applying all received log records, i.e., complete its redo, before accepting new writes, and must resolve any in-flight/ambiguous transactions at the failover boundary, conceptually mirroring undo of uncommitted work at the old primary that never reached the replica). The trade-offs here are consistency/durability vs. latency: synchronous log shipping (replica must acknowledge log receipt/apply before primary commits) guarantees zero data loss on failover (RPO = 0) at the cost of commit latency; asynchronous log shipping minimizes commit latency but admits a non-zero RPO window of committed-but-unreplicated transactions that are lost if the primary fails before shipping completes — this is the same fundamental trade-off as synchronous vs. asynchronous group commit within a single WAL, just extended across a network boundary.
